sections.h2: Where is Iowa City and what surrounds it?
sections.html:
Iowa City is on the Iowa River in eastern Iowa, along Interstate 80, about 60 miles west of the Quad Cities. It is the largest city in Johnson County and the county seat. The city sits at an elevation of about 656 feet.

The 2020 census counted 74,828 residents, which ranked it fifth in Iowa, and the metro area has more than 171,000 people. Coralville borders the city to the northwest, University Heights lies entirely inside the city limits, and nearby towns include Tiffin, North Liberty, Solon and Hills. Combined with Cedar Rapids, the region approaches 500,000 people.

The median age is 27.1, reflecting a large student population. Neighborhoods people mention often include the historic Northside near downtown, the Peninsula neighborhood and the east side.

sections.h2: What is the history behind Iowa City houses?
sections.html:
Iowa City was created by act of the Iowa Territory legislature on January 21, 1839, and incorporated on January 24, 1853. It served as the territorial capital from 1841 to 1846 and as the first state capital from 1846 to 1857, before the capital moved to Des Moines.

The Old Capitol, begun in 1839, is now a National Historic Landmark and museum. Its cupola burned in November 2001 and the building reopened in 2006. The University of Iowa was founded in 1847, so the city has had a campus-driven housing pattern for well over a century.

For a seller, the age of the house usually decides what an inspector or buyer looks at first, so it helps to know the year it was built before you talk to anyone.

sections.h2: Who are the biggest employers in Iowa City?
sections.html:
The University of Iowa and its hospital system dominate the local economy. The city's 2024 annual financial report lists these major employers:

The University of Iowa enrolls about 31,000 students, and its hospital is the state's only comprehensive tertiary care medical center.

sections.h2: How serious is flood risk in Iowa City?
sections.html:
Flood risk is real in parts of Iowa City, and the 2008 flood is the event buyers remember. Water passed the Coralville Reservoir's emergency spillway on June 11, 2008, and the Iowa River crested at a record 30.46 feet on June 13. Nineteen campus buildings were damaged.

The city requires a floodplain development permit in addition to a building permit for work in a flood hazard area. An elevation certificate is needed when a new structure is finished, when a remodel or repair costs 50 percent or more of the building's value, or when an addition increases floor area by 25 percent or more. New buildings must sit one foot above the 0.2 percent flood elevation.

Maps are also changing. The city says new FEMA maps took effect in August 2025, with flood heights dropping along Ralston Creek (which could take some properties out of the high-risk zone) and rising along Willow Creek (which could add some). Flood insurance is mandatory for federally backed loans on buildings in the 1 percent zone, and the city's participation in the Community Rating System gives an automatic 20 percent premium discount there.

  • Check the 2008 flood layer in the Johnson County GIS viewer to see whether a parcel was under water.
  • Call Neighborhood Development Services at 319-356-5120 for flood status and elevation certificates.
  • Ask your insurer how the new map changes your premium before you list.

sections.h2: What other weather matters to an Iowa City house?
sections.html:
Iowa City has a humid continental climate with hot summers and cold winters. The January average is about 22.8 degrees Fahrenheit and the July average about 75.8, with 38.47 inches of precipitation a year and 27.5 inches of snow. June is the wettest month.

An EF2 tornado struck on April 13, 2006, the first tornado recorded to hit the city directly. No one was killed, and damage was estimated at $12 million. Roofs, gutters and drainage therefore draw attention in inspections, and so do basements near Ralston Creek.

sections.h2: What rental permit rules apply in Iowa City?
sections.html:
Rental owners in Iowa City must hold a city rental permit, and that includes owner-occupied homes with more than one tenant. A landlord who sells the property should confirm the permit status with Housing Inspection Services.

The city's fee schedule lists $9 per bedroom, $17 per dwelling unit and $165 per structure, plus a $40 Certificate of Structural Compliance the first time. Bedrooms cannot exceed 35 percent of a dwelling's finished floor area, new bedrooms need at least 100 square feet and interconnected smoke alarms, and every unit door needs a deadbolt. The city also stopped allowing duplexes to function as one unit, so existing ones had to be permanently separated.

Continued complaints can lead to suspension of a landlord's permit under the city's Property Management Policy. Since July 2018 the review period for that policy has run 24 months instead of 12.

  • Gather permit and inspection records before you list a rental.
  • Resolve any open housing code notices, or disclose them.
  • Confirm the bedroom count on the permit matches the house.

sections.h2: Who assesses and collects property tax for an Iowa City house?
sections.html:
Houses inside Iowa City are assessed by the Iowa City Assessor, while the Johnson County Treasurer collects the tax. Residents outside the city limits deal with the Johnson County Assessor instead.

Real property is reassessed every two years in odd-numbered years, with a January 1 valuation date. A protest goes to the Board of Review between April 2 and April 30, and the board cannot extend that window. The assessor's office can be reached at 319-356-6066, Monday through Friday, 8:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m., and the page warns that its location can change during construction at the Administration Building.

The treasurer is at 913 S. Dubuque Street, Monday through Friday, 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., or at PO Box 2420, Iowa City, IA 52244-2420, and the phone is 319-356-6087. In 2026 the second half was due March 1 with penalties starting April 1 at 1.5 percent a month. Owners must also tell the assessor if a homestead is sold, and new homestead applications are due by July 1.

At closing, taxes are normally prorated, and the buyer is credited for the seller's share or the seller pays the treasurer. A transfer tax of eighty cents per $500 above the first $500 applies to deeds with value (Iowa Code 428A.1).

sections.h2: How do schools and transportation affect selling in Iowa City?
sections.html:
Public schools are run by the Iowa City Community School District, whose high schools are Iowa City High, Iowa City West, Liberty and Elizabeth Tate Alternative. Regina Catholic Education Center is a private PK-12 option.

Interstate 80 runs along the north edge of the city. U.S. 218 and Iowa 27 bypass it to the west, and U.S. 6 and Iowa 1 pass through. The Eastern Iowa Airport, about 20 miles northwest, has scheduled passenger flights. Local buses include Iowa City Transit, Coralville Transit and the university's Cambus, and the 380 Express commuter bus runs to Cedar Rapids.

sections.h2: How does a cash sale work for an Iowa City house?
sections.html:
A cash sale skips the lender, so an offer does not depend on an appraisal or loan approval. For a house with student-rental wear, an open permit or flood-related repairs, that can shorten the timeline.

You describe the house, receive a written offer, and decide. If you accept, a title company prepares the closing and settles taxes and any liens from the proceeds.

faqs.q: How many people live in Iowa City?
faqs.a: The 2020 census counted 74,828 residents. The city ranks fifth in Iowa, and the metro area has more than 171,000 people.

faqs.q: Does Iowa City have its own property assessor?
faqs.a: Yes. The Iowa City Assessor values houses inside the city limits, while the Johnson County Assessor covers areas outside it. Both belong to the Johnson County government site, and the Johnson County Treasurer collects the tax.

faqs.q: When can I protest an Iowa City property assessment?
faqs.a: Protests are filed with the Board of Review from April 2 through April 30 of the assessment year. The board cannot extend the deadline, and reassessments happen in odd-numbered years.

faqs.q: Do I need a rental permit to rent part of my Iowa City home?
faqs.a: Yes, if more than one tenant lives in an owner-occupied dwelling. The city's rental permit rules cover those homes along with other rentals.

faqs.q: Is Iowa City in a flood zone?
faqs.a: Parts of it are. The Iowa River flooded in June 2008, and new FEMA maps from August 2025 changed flood heights along Ralston Creek and Willow Creek. Check the specific parcel with Neighborhood Development Services.

faqs.q: Can I sell an Iowa City rental with tenants in place?
faqs.a: Yes. A buyer can take the house with tenants, subject to the lease and the city's rental permit rules, and the terms are spelled out in the purchase contract.
